chapters.title: The theme in one minute
chapters.readings: Bargoni et al. 2024, p. 1110; Quero & Ventura 2019, p. 48
paragraphs: In plain words, crowdfunding is many people giving small amounts to one project. The course treats it as more than money.

Bargoni and colleagues, 2024, make that point first. Crowdfunding is collective financing that also works as an instrument that supports innovation. It lets users act like venture capitalists, because they choose which projects go ahead.

Quero and Ventura, 2019, add the second half. A crowdfunding campaign is a service ecosystem, a setting where several actors cocreate value to carry one actor's proposal forward. The backer is not only a customer. The backer is part of the offer.
Why does the course include this in a course on innovation systems? Because it is a small system you can see whole. The actors are visible, the rules are short, and the value is easy to trace.
Remember: money from a crowd, and a small ecosystem where several actors make the value together.

checks.q: How does the course treat crowdfunding beyond money?
checks.a: As an instrument to foster innovation, and as a service ecosystem.

checks.q: What is a backer in a crowdfunding ecosystem?
checks.a: Part of the offer, not only a customer.

chapters.title: The key ideas
chapters.readings: Bargoni et al. 2024, pp. 1115, 1116; Quero & Ventura 2019, p. 52
paragraphs: Four ideas carry the theme.

The first is that crowdfunding can be innovative in two ways. Citing Chan and Parhankangas, Bargoni and colleagues, 2024, separate incremental innovativeness, which builds on what a firm already does, from radical innovativeness, which opens something genuinely new.
The second is openness. Citing Stanko and Henard, the same authors describe crowdfunding as an embodiment of open innovation, because it seeks ideas and support from outside the organisation.
The third is social capital. Citing Nahapiet and Ghoshal, they define it as the resources available through a network of relationships. A campaign runs on that network.

The fourth comes from Quero and Ventura, 2019. A value proposition is not fixed. Citing Frow and colleagues, they describe it as a mechanism that adjusts as actors negotiate how resources are shared, so the offer changes as the relationship changes.

Bargoni and colleagues, 2024, also map the field itself. Their review reduces more than two thousand records to one hundred and fifty studies, and it finds three clusters in the citations. One cluster is about innovativeness, one about openness, and one about platform innovation.
Remember: two kinds of innovativeness, openness, social capital and a value proposition that moves.

checks.q: What separates incremental from radical innovativeness?
checks.a: Incremental builds on what a firm already does, radical opens something genuinely new.

checks.q: Why is crowdfunding an example of openness?
checks.a: Because it seeks ideas and support from outside the organisation.

chapters.title: The model, step by step
paragraphs: There are two models.

The first is the five steps of value cocreation, adapted from Frow and Payne. First, identify the actors. Second, determine the core values. Third, open a dialogue between the actors. Fourth, identify the opportunities for cocreation. Fifth, cocreate the value propositions with the actors.

The second is the three levels of the ecosystem, following Chandler and Vargo. The micro level is direct exchange between two parties. The meso level is exchange that runs through a third party, such as a platform. The macro level is the wider network of institutions and associations.
There is also a list of eight ways to cocreate, the Eight Co's, which you can name if a question asks for detail. You do not need all eight to answer well.

The two models fit together. The five steps tell you what actors do, and the three levels tell you where they do it. If you have time in an exam, add one example at the micro level, because a small exchange is easier to describe than a whole platform.
Remember: five steps, three levels, and a list of eight ways to cocreate, and one small example to make it concrete.

checks.q: What are the five steps of value cocreation?
checks.a: Identify actors, determine values, facilitate dialogue, find opportunities and cocreate value propositions.
Exchange that runs through a third party, such as a platform.

chapters.title: Norway examples
chapters.readings: Demattos Guimarães et al. 2024, p. 8; Bonus, slide 42
paragraphs: The Norwegian material is thin, and you should say so.

Only one Norwegian example is verified in the course material. The bonus lecture shows that Norwegian crowdfunding grew from less than one million kroner in 2012 to almost nine hundred million in 2020, which is more than a thousand times.

The other studies do not use Norway. Demattos Guimarães and colleagues, 2024, map platforms in Europe and Latin America, and they code each platform on six dimensions, from country and geographical scope to business model, focus, institutional structure and foundation year. Quero and Ventura, 2019, study two Spanish platforms.

Use the Norwegian figure as your only Norwegian illustration, and use the platform studies for the concepts. A clear sentence about the limit of the material is worth more than an invented case. It also protects you. If the examiner asks for a Norwegian example and you have one figure, say what the figure measures and stop.
Remember: one Norwegian figure, and platform studies from other countries.

checks.q: What does the Norwegian figure show?
checks.a: Crowdfunding grew from less than one million kroner in 2012 to almost nine hundred million in 2020.

checks.q: Which countries do the platform studies cover?
checks.a: Europe and Latin America, and two Spanish platforms.

chapters.title: How the exam asks about it
paragraphs: The December question from 2024 asks how agency in innovation systems can promote or inhibit sustainable transformation. Crowdfunding communities are our own example here, and the course marks that clearly.

Here is the shape of a good answer. Say that you will read a crowdfunding community as one form of agency. Define the ecosystem, and name the actors: platforms, backers, creators and public institutions. Then use the five steps to show how a value proposition is negotiated.

Then answer both sides. Communities promote transformation when they move resources to projects that would not otherwise be funded, and when backers can see what their money supports. They inhibit transformation when a few platforms set the terms, or when a campaign rewards a familiar name rather than a new idea.
One caution. The paper on platforms and the paper on value cocreation do not study sustainability. Say that your reading is an application, and you keep the answer honest.

A second move is to name the actors in order. Start with the platform, which sets the terms. Then the creator, who brings the proposal. Then the backers, who bring money and judgement. Then the public institutions, which the Spanish directors added to the list. When the actors are named, the value proposition is easy to describe.
Remember: define the ecosystem, show the negotiation, and mark your application as your own reading.

checks.q: How do you mark the crowdfunding example?
checks.a: As our own reading, not as a finding of the papers.

checks.q: When do crowdfunding communities inhibit transformation?
checks.a: When a few platforms set the terms, or a familiar name beats a new idea.

chapters.title: Test yourself
chapters.readings: Bargoni et al. 2024, p. 1121; Quero & Ventura 2019, p. 60
paragraphs: Question one. What makes a crowdfunding campaign a service ecosystem?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Several actors cocreate value around one proposal, and the value proposition adjusts as they negotiate. The backer is part of the offer.
Question two. What are the three levels of an ecosystem, and what sits at the meso level?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Micro, meso and macro. The meso level is exchange that runs through a third party, such as a platform.
Question three. Why should you call the sustainability reading your own?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Because the crowdfunding papers do not study sustainability. The link to transformation is an application, and saying so keeps the answer honest.
Remember: a small ecosystem with visible actors, a value proposition under negotiation, and a link to sustainability that you mark as your own.

checks.q: Who sets the terms in a crowdfunding ecosystem?
checks.a: The platforms, which is why a few of them can shape what gets funded.

checks.q: What do the five steps produce?
checks.a: A value proposition that the actors cocreate together.
